The method we were taught at culinary trade school for seasoning cast iron pans is to start by filling the base with fine salt and placing over medium-high heat for a few minutes, stirring the salt around to pick up any moisture and dirt, also this will act as a light abrasive and even out tiny imperfections in the surface a bit.

After this, pour out the salt (careful that shit will be hot!) and rub use a paper towel that has just enough canola oil to be damp.

Use either tongs or gloves as the pan should be hot and you will be returning it to the heat until the oil has blackened (around 250 deg C, if you're a pedantic prick like me use a cheap I.R thermometer to make sure you are at the right range), taking it above 330 deg C is too high and the non-stick properties won't be anywhere near as good.

Although some chefs do the first coat at higher temps and then drop the temp down gradually for further coats, personally I don't notice a difference, but chefs can be wankers, myself included.

Repeat the oil process a few times to build up a solid layer. Don't deglaze your pan using wine or vinegars and avoid cooking acidic based foods in it.

If this still doesn't make your pan non-stick, then it most likely has an uneven surface and will require grinding to level it.
